utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Judge Kinis and myself informed the parties that Judge Gwaunza, for personal reasons, is unable to attend. We have considered whether or not to continue the proceedings, and we concluded that it's in the interests of justice to continue the proceedings in the absence of Judge Gwaunza under Rule 15 bis. Then I have one other matter which I'd like to raise. On the 9th of October, the Chamber has indicated in court that it was considering the complex legal issue of relying on sections of a 92 ter statement from which a witness had distanced himself, in whole or in part, also in light of the case law developed at this Tribunal on previous inconsistent statements. On that day, the Chamber had initial oral submissions from the Gotovina Defence and the Prosecution in this matter and invited the parties to make any submissions they wished. On the 12th of October, the Gotovina Defence indicated in court that it was prepared to address the matter further, and the Chamber stated it would like to hear from the other parties when they were ready. The Chamber now invites the parties to file written submissions, if they wish to do so, by the 28th of October, 2009, on the practical implications of the developed case law on previous inconsistent statements on the admission of sections of 92 ter statements that were not attested or not fully attested to in court. That's the invitation of the Chamber. And then we'll wait for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cipci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Are you ready, Mr. Kay, to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm just looking at matters in paragraph 17 of the witness's statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, in your statement, you said that you found out Mr. Cermak was sent to Knin to take care of everything with regard to the normalisation of life of the civilians that remained in that area, and you said that: "This is what I was told by the MUP." I'd like to ask you some questions about that, more specifically as to any discussions you may have had or how this information came to you. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect when you first heard about Mr. Cermak's position of being sent to Knin for the normalisation of life? Can you recollect when you first heard that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can recollect that very well. It was on the 6th. On the 5th, I entered Knin, and the president was supposed to come on the 6th. Franjo Tudjman was supposed to come. On the 6th, in the morning, I was in Knin because it was to be assumed that they would continue to Kijevo. On the 6th, my minister, Ivan Jarnjak came, and the assistant minister, Josko Moric, also came. I heard that they had arrived. I believe that I even saw Mr. Cermak when he arrived, and then I immediately asked my minister, Mr. Jarnjak, what Mr. Cermak's function was. Given the fact that I already had a hundred policemen stationed in Knin, I was curious to know who I could contact from the army in case my employees, who were deployed in Knin, needed something. And they were under the command of the Knin Administration, whose name I believe was Mr. -- well, I don't know. Romanic, Romanic. And that was when Mr. Jarnjak -- when the minister first told me that the arrival of Mr. Cermak in Knin was exclusively to take care of the normalisation of life in the territory of Knin. He also told me that Mr. Cermak enjoyed the status of the garrison commander. From my previous contacts with the garrison commander of Split, which was much larger, I knew what his authorities were. Mr. Cermak, irrespective of his rank of a general that he acquired much earlier, he could not have any higher authorities than the garrison commander of Split, which was much larger and which comprised several combat units; the command of the Croatian Navy; and two battalions of the military police, the 72nd and the 73rd Battalions. Should I tell you something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just wait there, please, because I've had a note that the transcriber and interpreter are struggling, and they have to keep up with you, Mr. Cipci, to relay this information to us and others. And I could tell that they were speaking very, very quickly. So I tend to speak fairly slowly in court, and that's because it's being translated. Can you remember to do that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Thank you. [Interpretation] I will speak very slowly for the benefit of both the interpreters and the transcriber. I really want them to do their job well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You gave us a lot of information there, and I'll go back to look at some parts of it with you. You told us that you had a hundred policemen in Knin, and you were curious to know who you could contact from the army because your employees were deployed there under Mr. Romanic. And you were told by Mr. Jarnjak about Mr. Cermak's task to exclusively take care of the normalisation of life in Knin, and he was the garrison commander. Now, if we just look at parts of that, first of all. Were your employees, the hundred or so policemen from your police administration, to have any contact or to be subordinated to Mr. Cermak in any way?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not supposed to have any contact with him. They were directly subordinated to Mr. Romanic. Romanic was subordinated to Cetina, and Cetina was subordinated to Jarnjak. That was the hierarchy of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, taking that day of the 6th of August, was there any suggestion in the information you received that Mr. Romanic was to be subordinated under the command of General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No information to that effect at all. Mr. Romanic, on the 6th, was appointed as a temporary chief of the Police Administration of Knin. On the following day, I believe it was the 7th, I officially inaugurated him, together with the assistant minister for the SZUP, and I believe that together with us was the chief of the Police Administration of Sibenik, Mr. Matic. I believe that official documents for Mr. Romanic arrived at the time, and we officially installed him in his new office. That was Mr. Smiljan Reljic, the assistant minister for SZUP. "SZUP" is the abbreviation standing for the Office for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. Am I still too fast?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I hesitate to say it, but you are. But you're doing better.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Break, I better take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, now, looking into that information that you gave us concerning Mr. Romanic, you said that you appointed him or inaugurated him into his position. Had you previously had a relationship with Mr. Romanic, in the sense that he had worked for you?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I met Mr. Romanic on that day when Mr. Smiljan Reljic, Mr. Matic, and I arrived in Knin. We found him on the staircase of the Police Administration. He was sitting there because he has his office there as the chief of the Police Administration. Previously, Knin never had its own administration. There was just a police station there prior to that. On that day, I met Mr. Romanic for the first time ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. It was the inauguration, what you meant by that, that I wanted an explanation for, that you said on the next day, the 7th. Could you explain to the Court what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was that I had received a telephone call by Minister Jarnjak. He told me to go to Sibenik to find Chief Matic, then to go to Drnis to the birthplace of Mr. Smiljan Reljic - he was there at the time - and then the three of us were supposed to go to Knin. That's where we would be met by Mr. Romanic, and that we would then officially introduce him to his new office. That was the formal inauguration of Mr. Romanic. I suppose that Mr. Smiljan Reljic also brought the official documents on the appointment of Mr. Romanic on him, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm still going back to that very first long answer you gave me, and I want to go back to something you mentioned concerning -- you knew about the garrison because you were based in Split. Is that where your police administration headquarters were, in Split?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters of the Police Administration, its building, were in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you aware of there being a garrison, then, in Split, the Split Garrison?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only was I aware, not only was I aware, I was personal friends with Mr. Zoricic, who was the garrison commander of Split, and we're still friends. I believe he had the rank of either major or brigadier. I'm not sure. I knew that. We would occasionally meet, socialise as friends on private matters always.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, in relation to his position as Split Garrison commander, did he have any command or authority over the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I would just like to say two sentences about that. When I assumed my duties as the chief of the Police Administration, I studied the legal documents relative to my job, so I studied laws and bylaws relative to the work of the Ministry of the Interior. Since it was war and I had the 4th Guards Brigade in Split and two Home Guards Battalions, I had the headquarters of the Croatian Navy. There was also the 72nd Battalion of the Military Police and the 73rd Battalion of the Military Police, obviously I studied the laws that were relative to the system and work of the Croatian Army. I was interested in finding about the relationship between the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence. And it is just because I studied all that, I arrived at a conclusion very easily, because it is explicitly stated in the laws, that a garrison commander has no authority whatsoever over the combat units deployed in his area. And it is for that reason that throughout the four years of war, never, ever had a single official meeting with the Split Garrison commander, Mr. Zoricic. However, I very often communicated with him privately, unlike -- in that case, I had frequent contacts with the commander of the 4th Brigade, General Krsticevic, Admiral Letica, the commander of the Croatian Navy. I also had contacts with the commanders of the Home Guards Brigade. I had contacts with the commander of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I could give you some guidance. Once the text on the screen stops moving, that means that the transcriber has up to that moment finished the transcript, and she [sic] does that on the basis of the translation of your words, the interpretation of your words. So if you'd have a look on your screen now and then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the left side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the moving screen, to say so. I take it, Madam Usher, that the witness can look at the English text as well. And if you would develop a speed of speech, something between Mr. Kay and myself, that would be ideal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think we may have missed some information concerning your contacts with the commanders of the Home Guards Brigade, and "I had contacts with the commander of ..." Can you recollect the other contacts you wanted to refer to after you mentioned the commanders of the Home Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will gladly do that. I had contacts with all the commanders of military units, including Admiral Sveto Letica, and that was for a simple reason. My function and position was in the County of Split and Dalmatia, which was covered by the Police Administration of Split and Dalmatia, and that comprised the city of Split, 12 other cities, and many municipalities. It was my task to look after order and safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And for that very reason, for that very reason, I had contacts with the commanders in order to establish normal relations with them that would enable me to avoid, in a peaceful way, all possible incidents that might have arised [as interpreted] as a result of a huge number of soldiers deployed in my area. In addition to the troops, through my police administration, I had frequent passages of HVO soldiers from Bosnia. I also had the command of international forces that was headquartered there together with a big logistical centre, and for that very reason I also had frequent contacts with the commander of the international forces, whose command was some 10 kilometres away from Split. And a large logistic base was in the north or cargo harbour of the city of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you for that detail. There's one matter I want to ask you about, which was your contact with the 72nd and 73rd military police battalions, and I'm still going back to your first answer you gave me. And what was your reason for having contact with them, as the chief of the Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, although I was the chief of the Police Administration, I had to define all the relations between the military police that was stationed in Split and the civilian police. I wanted to have some coordination in the performance of our tasks. And the reason was this: At that time, our judiciary system -- our overall judiciary system was divided into two parts, the military, and -- on the one hand, and the civilian on the other. We had the military police, the Military Prosecutor's Office, and military courts; and, on the other hand, we had the civilian police, the Civilian Prosecutor's Office, and civilian courts. Since they were not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. The Court has heard a lot of evidence about that and is familiar with the structure, and I thank you for giving the information, but we already know that and the Judges have already had a great deal of evidence about that, with Your Honour's leave -- if Your Honour agrees with that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may take that course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to move now to another area, and that concerns paragraph 23 of your statement and an issue concerning passes and Mr. Cermak. If we could look at D -- Exhibit D497, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I cannot see on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It will come eventually.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is a document dated the 16th of August. We're still waiting for the English to come onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's from the Ministry of Interior, Split-Dalmatia Police Administration, and it's signed by you, dated the 16th of August, 1995, and it's sent to Operation Povratak staff in Zagreb and had an attachment with it. Do you recognise this document that we have here as being a document written by you?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document on the screen bears my signature. I sent this letter to the ministry and the HQ of Operation Povratak, although I do not see what the document attached to this letter was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll now look at that. If we could turn to the next page, please. And we can see the document headed the 16th of August, 1995, and its subject is the report on the presence of members of the EC Monitoring Mission in the area of Vrlika. And looking at the text, if you can look at what was written, it concerns a telegram, informing the identity of people in the Croatia -- as members of the ECMM, which was found out through an interview of them. The names of the people and where they're from is set out, as well as a vehicle and what their business was, that they'd been stopped at a check-point when they were entering Vrlika.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 3 in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And they visited the commander of the Kenyan Battalion stationed in Civljane, who informed them about mass graves in villages of Cetina and Jezevic, and it concerned whether they had a permit in the area. And they were told to go back in the direction of Knin to obtain it. And it says there what they wanted to do, and refers that they were informed by another team in their group, in their hierarchy, that they had a certificate issued by General Cermak allowing free movement of the entire ECMM in the Croatian area, and they were told that at an interview. And that was signed by you in this report. Do you recollect the information in this report and the particular incident?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recall many things, but a number of years have passed in the meantime, and I'm not a young boy anymore, either. I simply recall these details because I had announced to Mr. Cermak prior to this that in case I find anyone in my area of responsibility requiring my pass, with his pass on that person, that that person would be removed from my area of responsibility. And following that announcement, I did this: There were other persons similar to these from the international community who arrived after Operation Storm, always had with them an approval of the Ministry of Defence. I think it was Markica Rebic or General Tolj who issued such documents and who were in contact with representatives of the international community. Such approvals went through the Ministry of the Interior and down to me, if they were to go through my area, or if they were to spend some time in my area. In such cases, I would provide them with the required passes. If the Presiding Judge would allow me, I would like to add something. Before Operation Storm, at the level of the Ministry of the Interior, we had held several meetings at which it was clearly defined in which way check-points would be set up and who was to issue passes to whom, in terms of movement. It was said then that for all civilian personnel, they fell exclusively under the authority of the chief of the Police Administration in whose territory the aforementioned check-point was. We were not interested in military personnel because we had no right to stop them. We couldn't stop either the military personnel or vehicles. It was irrelevant for me who was issuing permits for military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what was the problem with a certificate given by General Cermak to allow the ECMM to go anywhere they liked in Croatia? What was the problem for you as to why you rejected it?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were problematic because these were civilians, irrespective of the fact that they were foreigners. They were not military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just go back to the second page, and we see handwritten on the right-hand side a series of names: Moric, Reljic, Benko, Zidovec.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moric was assistant minister for the basic duty police. Reljic was another assistant minister for the SZUP, Benko was in charge of the crime police, and Zidovec was the head of the Legal Affairs Department. All these were officials of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to assist as to why they would be copied in on this particular report and the information that you have within it, why it would be going to those people?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say. It seems to me that all these people or, rather, the different sectors within the ministry were regularly involved in the events after Operation Storm. Reljic, as the assistant minister for the protection of the constitutional order, as well as Benko, who was assistant minister for the crime police, because many things had to be done in the area of Knin in order to deal with criminal and legal matters, prosecutions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did any of those four people go to the Knin area as a part of their duties at various times?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Reljic was, on the 5th or the 6th, already in the area of the Krajina, because he hails from Drnis. It was logical for him to go and visit his home and his area. He was there for that reason, and also for official business, probably. Mr. Moric, I suppose, was in Knin on the 6th when Mr. -- when President Tudjman was there, and I suppose he came after that as well, although we did not meet. I don't know for Mr. Benko, whether he was there or not. I do know, however, that he sent some of his men to Sibenik and Zadar because they were tasked with processing many legal and criminal matters there. I also gave my chief of sector of the crime police at the disposal of Mr. Benko - he was one of the best experts in Croatia - so that he could help his colleagues in Zadar, Sibenik, and Split. Zidovec, since he was in charge of legal and administrative matters, went down there occasionally, although we didn't meet. Katica Osrecki, who was assistant minister for finance, also went there. And in the course of the first few days after Operation Storm, we went to see Mr. Cermak together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have a record of the name on the transcript of the assistant minister for finance. Perhaps if you could repeat the name you gave of the person you went to see Mr. Cermak with.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Katica Osrecki.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you remember what the purpose of meeting Mr. Cermak was with her?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a private meeting, because Ms. Katica Osrecki knew Mr. Cermak from before. When she arrived in the area, she asked me to accompany her, since she was not familiar with Knin. It was in the first few days after Operation Storm. I took her there. It was a solely private meeting of Ms. Osrecki and Mr. Cipci with Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to, then, the refusal of entry of those members of the ECMM, who had permission from Mr. Cermak, were you aware of the agreement that had been signed on the 6th of August between Mr. Akashi, on behalf of the United Nations, and Mr. Sarinic, on behalf of the Croatian government, which gave freedom of movement to various parts of the UNCRO forces that were in Croatia for various purposes? Were you and your police administration aware of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I think I was familiar with the agreement. But could you assist me, perhaps, and tell me when the agreement was signed, the agreement between Sarinic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was signed on the 6th of August, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you would like to see a copy of it, it is Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That won't be necessary. Very well. However, as far as I can recall, 15 years later, I think in practice it did function in a way that all those members of different monitoring and other international forces turned to the Ministry of Defence, which was the only body authorised to allow access to certain areas during wartime conditions. I think it went through such people as Rebic and Tolj. They would issue their approvals, and then that would go down the chain, allowing those people to visit. I remember that on the 6th already, and in the next few days, I used to see International Monitors in their white vehicles moving about the Krajina. One of them would usually drive and another one sitting on the hood, taping what was going on. I saw that myself on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask was: Did you appreciate, in rejecting the ECMM monitors who had said that Mr. Cermak had given them permission to go where they like, that they were people who were entitled to go where they like, under the Akashi-Sarinic Agreement of the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not in dispute that they could move, but still all of them had to have a paper, a document which would confirm their identity and contain their notification of intent to enter such delicate areas. They had to notify those competent, and then, in turn, they could visit the area. We could not deny issuing them passes. That is the gist of the agreement between the Croatian government and Mr. Sarinic and them. We had obligations on our part, whereas their obligation was to notify us on time and to request a permission to enter that area. This is how I interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to look at another document which is another form of pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D494, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you will see on the screen a letter dated the 15th of August, 1995, from you, as chief of the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration, to Operation Povratak staff in Zagreb. And the letter submits a copy of a pass for entering the Knin Garrison, issued by the Knin Garrison Command, and seeking a reply and confirming in writing the validity of the passes for civilian persons in question. First of all, do you recollect this letter as having been written by you?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I wrote this letter. And I also recall that Mr. Cermak, during a private visit which took place immediately after Operation Storm, showed me a printed pass which he produced in order to allow persons freedom of movement in the liberated area. I told Mr. Cermak immediately that such passes issued to civilians would be considered invalid in my area of responsibility. Pursuant to that, I sent a letter to the HQ of Operation Povratak to which a copy of such pass issued by Mr. Cermak was attached. I received their reply, in which it said that Mr. Cermak's passes are only valid for military personnel and not for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could just look at this document, first of all, and we see handwriting on it which is translated as being: "By checking through the Knin Police Administration, Colonel-General Cermak will issue an order on the annulment of and free movement of civilians. "It must come in writing from the Ministry of Defence." First of all, do you know who wrote that on your letter?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the monitor, I cannot see the signature, but I do recognise the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we lift it up to -- sorry, the other way, so we can see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's illegible, it's too dark. I suppose, given that I had sent it to the HQ, and Mr. Moric was in charge of the HQ of Operation Povratak, this could have been written by him, or perhaps this note was written by an associate of Mr. Moric who at that time happened to be in the headquarters. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see what letters of the signature are represented there? Are you able to interpret them for us as to what those particular letters are?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that this could be "J.M.," his initials, at least from what I can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said in your answer that you could recognise the handwriting. Are you able to give us any more information on that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was trying to say that I cannot recognise the handwriting, but the initials appear to me to be "J.M.," which could, in turn, be Josko Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to help us at all about the checks made through the Knin Police Administration? Do you know anything about that in relation to this matter concerning checking the validity of the pass?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the note, itself, which says: "By checking through the Knin PU, Colonel General Cermak ..." and so on, I cannot confirm that because I don't know who General Cermak spoke to or Josko Moric spoke to, but it can be supposed that Josko Moric called the chief of the Police Administration in Knin, who in turn spoke to Mr. Cermak, but that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can now look at Exhibit D495.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is this a copy of the pass that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this -- this has some handwriting on it?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says it only applies to military personnel and civilians working in the Croatian Army. This is in accordance to what I had told Mr. Cermak. Civilians can only move through my check-points with my approval, as well as military personnel and civilians enjoying the status of Croatian Army members could move with his passes in such areas we -- in which he believed they were supposed to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you know who wrote the information on this pass that we have here? First of all, the first bit about "according to the MUP staff announcement, it is valid only for military personnel and civilians working in the Croatian Army." Do you know who wrote that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that you're asking me too much at this point. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not from your office, then?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This obviously came from General Cermak's office. In the first sentence, it says: "According to the MUP staff announcement," which is the HQ of Operation Povratak, headed by Mr. Josko Moric to whom I had sent my query on the validity of Cermak's passes, and he says: "According to the MUP staff announcement, it is valid only for military personnel and civilians working for the Croatian Army." Therefore, it is clear that Mr. Cermak's office received an official notification of Povratak HQ on their right -- or, rather, the absence of their right to issue passes to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recollect yesterday we looked at one document, Exhibit D496, which was also dated the 15th of August, 1995, and it was a document sent by you concerning the passengers on the Split-Knin traffic line? Do you recollect us looking at that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. We discussed that yesterday. We discussed my inquiry as to whether it was possible to exert further control over the journey of all those who were interested in getting on that train, and the passes, and the abolishment of the passes. I remember that there was a document on the monitor yesterday that I looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So in relation to the Cermak passes we've looked at and your document dated the 15th of August, are you able to tell us, then, what the policy was of the Ministry of Interior, Operation Povratak Group, in relation to the need for passes to go into the liberated territories?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in agreement before Operation Storm, it was said that police check-points should be established and that we should reach an agreement with the military police to have mixed patrols on the check-points in order to exert control over civilians and military personnel. As far as civilians went, the passes should have been issued in a very restrictive manner, which means that in the liberated area we could have the return of people enjoying the status of refugees. They were supposed to have passes; furthermore, all civilians that had a job to do in respect of the normalisation of the situation in Knin. And I issued passes to all such personnel, and I'm talking about the employees of electrical companies, posts, television, radio, banks, and similar institutions. Other persons who had a private business, who wanted to go for curiosity or emotional reasons, could not be issued passes to go to the liberated area. Even my employees, who did not have an official job to do in the liberated area, could not go through my check-points, either in civilian clothes or in uniform, without my pass. I know that an employee of mine from Makarska who set out to go up there was placed under disciplinary procedures because he had crossed the check-point and entered the territory of Knin without my pass. In other words, I had a very restrictive criteria when it came to the issuing of passes to go to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just so that we can look at something to reflect that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have 2D00760, please. While we're waiting for it to come up, Your Honour, may I have leave to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were referring to the passes you issued. Do you recognise this as being one such pass for the team from the electrical company who were --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- surveying repairs?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hold on, hold on. Let's take it step by step. This pass was assigned, as far as I can see, by my deputy, because it says here "assistant" or "deputy chief," and this is not my signature. This is either Petar Pasic's signature or -- I believe that he signed this. However, judging by the content, I would say that this reflects the form of the passes that were issued to persons who had a job to do in Knin. This was issued to the employees of the Split Bank, the officials of the television, post, radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no need to ask you more about that, save to ask that it be made an exhibit, with Your Honour's leave. MS. DE LANDRI: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours. Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1724.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1724 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm now moving to another subject, Mr. Cipci. From your statement, it seems that you regularly visited the Knin region during this period, after Operation Storm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went there very often, especially during the first few days. On the 5th, in the morning, I entered Knin. I was in Knin on the 6th, very early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm asking you now about after that period. Later on, did your visits to Knin continue, to the Knin region? I'm not just talking about the town. I'm talking about Knin and the area around it.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after that I did go to the liberated area, not as often as during the initial period during the first few days. And the reason for that was very simple. In the area of Knin, in addition to the employees who were in Knin already on the 5th, over the course of time I added to them a large number of my employees in the Police Administration. There were employees from my administration working on documents, issuing passes, in an office that was called Administrative Office. They issued documents to people who applied for them, and they also arranged the archives. I also provided a lot of commanders of police stations, such as the one in Drnis, Srb, Lapac, I don't know how many of them. Several of such police stations were covered by my men. And since they were only kids and they were scared and they did not have enough logistical support, I visited them for two reasons: Firstly, to show them that I, as an elderly man, was able to come to the area, that they, as young lads, should not be afraid; and, secondly, I would also take my big Range Rover and take as much logistical things as I could. Those were the reasons why I quite frequently moved around Krajina, through the liberated area. I visited my employees, irrespective of the fact that they were under the authority of Mr. Romanic. But I was the one who had sent them there, and I considered myself responsible enough to take care of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you cooperate and coordinate with other senior police officers who were in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Romanic was the one. I met him. And after that, we did not see each other that often. I did not feel the need to talk to him that much. He was subordinated to Mr. Cetina, the chief of Zadar Administration, not me. And in factual terms, we were just colleagues, nothing else. And when I arrived in Knin, I would visit my employees, my men, who were working in the secondary school. And I would also pay a visit to the administrative and legal office that was staffed with my employees who were working there on arranging documents and issuing personal documents to applicants. And then I would go -- I would proceed to one of the stations where I also had my men deployed. I would go and visit them. I would go to see them. And that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have contacts with coordinators who were appointed by the Ministry of Interior, Operation Povratak, in Zagreb, who were appointed to assist the Police Administrations and -- in the region?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the headquarters or, rather, the ministry did send a certain number of employees to assist down there. I knew those people, but I did not feel any need to contact them. They were either sent to assist the Police Administration of Knin, or they came from the crime police, and they were sent to Zadar and Sibenik because there were criminal proceedings instituted against people who committed certain things after Operation Storm in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So in relation to what you were doing, then, in the Knin region at that time as your police work and the contacts that you had, what would you say about the allegation that Mr. Cermak was in command of the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you have to understand that the area of the Knin Administration was not within my jurisdiction. All my visits to Knin and the liberated area can be considered semi-private, irrespective of the fact that I arrived in police uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the microphones that are not in use please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, as far as I know, I can say with certainty that Mr. Cermak, in respect of the civilian police, did not have any authority whatsoever because the commander of the Split Garrison also did not have any jurisdiction over the military police, let alone the civilian police. Mr. Cermak discharged the duties of the garrison commander in keeping with the law that was in effect at that time. He could not have any higher authorities whatsoever than Mr. Zoricic, who was the garrison commander in Split, irrespective of the difference in ranks. Their authorities were not determined by their ranks, but by the law, and the authorities that were prescribed by the law were exactly the authorities that Mr. Cermak had. And those authorities did not entail any right to command over the civilian police, just to the contrary. As far as I can remember, from the law that I perused at that time, the garrison commander was duty-bound to establish quality cooperation with the civilian authorities and the civilian police. And that applied to Mr. Cermak as well. He was duty-bound to establish quality cooperation with Mr. Romanic, not myself. He could only establish a good, friendly relationship with me on the two occasions that we met. But as far as his authorities go, in comparison with the authorities of Mr. Zoricic, I can say that he could not have any authorities with respect to the civilian police, either in factual terms or under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever have any indication or any information given to you that he was attempting to influence the police in any way?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard any such thing. However, it would be very normal and very clear to me that faced with the circumstances that Mr. Cermak and Mr. Romanic encountered, as well as the government's commissioner, Mr. Petar Pasic, and the circumstances were riddled with a delicate situation. I'm sure that they had to have permanent, daily cooperation, and that as a result of that joint cooperation, they were able to deal with some basic problems. On the 5th, when my hundred men arrived in Knin, that same evening I had to send them a tank of drinking water and a generator to give them light because there was no water or electricity in Knin, and that's the situation that Mr. Cermak, Mr. Romanic, and Mr. Petar Pasic found when they arrived in Knin. And I understand and I appreciate that they had to have daily contacts and that they had to rely on each other for the job to be done properly and for the situation in Knin to be normalised as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If Mr. Cermak had issued a written order to the police in Knin, would the police have been obliged to follow such a written order?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, and I'm speaking from my police experience: If Mr. Cermak had issued any official order, they would not have been binding upon the police. I could issue an official order to my minister of foreign affairs because -- and that would amount to nothing because he was not my subordinate. And Romanic was not subordinated to Mr. Cermak, by the same token. However, if Mr. Romanic found a crime was committed in the area where he was working, it was his duty to inform the Police Administration what had happened, and that applied to every citizen who learned about a crime. They were supposed to report it to the police, and then the police would have taken whatever was necessary to deal with that. In other words, if Mr. Cermak had issued an order of any kind to carry out a preliminary proceedings because of a crime, that was nothing by notification. The police has to react to any report by private persons, even if it is anonymous. The police will still carry out certain procedures to investigate. If such a report is signed by a person, if it contains an address and a telephone number, the police has to make all the checks. Otherwise, there could be disciplinary proceedings instituted against the person who failed to do that. So when we're talking about orders to the police that Mr. Cermak might have sent to Mr. Romanic, if he did, then those were notifications. If Mr. Cermak sent any order to the police - I don't know why he should have done that - I assume that that order was drafted on his behalf in his office and then he only signed it, because I can only assume that Mr. Cermak, when he took over the duties as the garrison commander, he should have taken the law and he should have read the provisions of the law in terms of his rights and obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just in your answer there, we've noted on the transcript that it says: "However, if Mr. Romanic found a crime was committed in the area where he was working, it was his duty to inform the Police Administration what had happened ..." Did you mean Mr. Cermak rather than Mr. Romanic, because Mr. Romanic was the Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every person in a certain position in state office has more responsibility than an ordinary person, so if a garrison commander learns about something that happened, he's duty-bound to inform everybody who has the official capacity to carry out certain proceedings to establish the facts. Therefore, that would be a moral obligation of every citizen. But if you're a civil servant, then it is not just moral obligation, it is your responsibility as a civil servant. And then, yes, I said "Mr. Cermak."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And just finishing with this matter, would Mr. Cermak have had any disciplinary powers over the police?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said it already. He did not have any powers. And if I said that he did not have any powers, that also comprises disciplinary powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Wait. Others may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I please say just one sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what is in that sentence. But please say the sentence, and then we'll see what the relevance of it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just going to say this: Most of the questions put to me, and my answers to the questions, could be obtained if you consulted the laws of the Republic of Croatia that were passed at the time. You will find it there, everything about the responsibilities and duties of every single official. And that's the long and the short of my sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This Chamber has heard quite some evidence in relation to legislation which was adopted. This Chamber has also heard that sometimes practice was not for the full 100 per cent in line with what the laws told us, and therefore we appreciate that you answer the questions, and we'll certainly not ignore existing legislation. I think it's most practical if we first have the break and then give an opportunity to the other Defences and the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Kehoe, and I'm looking at you and also at the Prosecution, the next witness in line, I think, is on standby. Does that witness need to remain on standby? Is there any chance that we'll have substantial time, that means more than 15 minutes, for that witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see three persons standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I had consulted the parties earlier, and I've also had the advantage of looking at disclosed exhibit lists for cross-examination, and in my view the witness should be sent home and come back after the break, and given a proper time-period then, as he's a substantial witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what would that mean for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think this witness will be going into tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not the whole time, but a substantial amount, and we do have some MFIs to clear up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To my mind, it didn't make sense starting a substantial witness, then having what would be a three- or four-week break, maybe, before we'd reach him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least -- we will not be sitting for at least 10 or 11 days on from Thursday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and we have fixed witnesses for that week and the week after. Experts have been booked to attend. So my idea was to put him right at the very end and fit him in as virtually the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the other parties, whether there's any disagreement in the assessment that we would not be able to -- apart from starting today, that it would not even be wise, perhaps, to start tomorrow. MS. DE LANDRI: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still, to send a witness home is something one would not easily do. Have you considered, Mr. Kay, any other options? Although I don't think that we could sit tomorrow in the afternoon, and that would not be sufficient either, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is a substantial witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been given thorough thought, and then the witness is excused for the time being. He doesn't -- well, you leave that -- I leave that in your hands with the Witnesses and Victims Section, and we are now aware of the consequences as far as scheduling is concerned. Then, Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Cipci?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cipci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, if we could put Mr. Cipci's statement, D1723, on the screen, and direct our attention to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cipci, I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 4 and ask you several preliminary questions prior to -- or that go to the planning prior to Operation Storm on the 4th of August. Now, you received direction from Minister Jarnjak that you were to prepare yourself to move into the liberated areas as quickly as possible in order to get that area under control, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as part of that, you note, in paragraph 5, that you, in fact, garnished more than the number of police officers that you actually -- excuse me, in paragraph 6, you had three times as many police officers as necessary to do that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, was there ever any indication, in your discussions with Minister Jarnjak or with Assistant Minister Moric, that the MUP was to allow criminal activity to take place? I ask you that question, sir, because I just need your answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was never any mention of that. It is precisely the police who are there to prevent the commission of crimes, to act as prevention, or to sanction the crimes committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Cipci, with that goal in mind, did you understand that Minister Jarnjak's and Assistant Minister Moric's instructions to you were to -- and to other administration chiefs, that the instructions were to you to move quickly to secure the area and to prevent the commission of crime?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Minister Jarnjak, and I don't think Moric ever attended those meetings with police chiefs, with Minister Jarnjak, on two or three occasions, we discussed extensively our obligations once Operation Storm commences. The legal provisions task the police with securing law and order, as well as protecting the lives and property of people in that area. In keeping with the Law on the Interior, we were duty-bound, upon liberation, to enter the area with the necessary number of police in order to meet our legal obligations. Regarding my area of responsibility, I acted slightly differently because I had had certain bad experience in the course of World War II when there were four armies, two opposing sides, and two liberating forces entered my city. All four armed forces, be it occupational or liberation forces, behaved the same way. They killed and looted. That is why, having had that experience, I presumed that a similar or the same thing could happen this time as well, once the Croatian Army liberates its territory. It was clear to me that there was a very high degree of hatred, amounting to pathological hatred, I would dare say, and I presumed that spontaneous revenge or instances of revenge could occur against everything --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, let me cut you a little short.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And based on your instructions and your experience, you moved very quickly into your sector, and specifically Vrlika, and on the 5th of August you established the police station, as you say in paragraph 5 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I moved in very quickly, but I even ordered my police sector chief, Mr. Urija, to have the police units, which were at the ready, as well as a number of people sufficient to man a police station, together with a sign that would be put onto the building. I ordered him to move into Vrlika together with the Croatian Army. I undertook the effort of accompanying my force to enter Vrlika together with the army, because I wanted to be in my area of responsibility in Vrlika simultaneously with the Croatian Army so that I could take over full control over the area I was responsible for immediately. We set up a police station. We covered the area, set up check-points. And in agreement with the commanders of those units which were there from the Croatian Army, after a very short ceremony, left my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me cut you short so I can just -- so I can move in the interests of time. And let me show you a document on that score, which is 65 ter 1D2991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is your report of 5 August 1995, reporting the establishment of the police -- excuse me, the police substation in Vrlika by 1600 hours on the 5th, and also notifying other branch substations, and that the "previously occupied territory of this police administration is under control." Is that an accurate assessment of what you did at that particular juncture, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? What is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you recall this -- this particular report and that you sent something similar to this at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all reports which came out of my police administration were not written by me, not all of them. As you can see, there is no signature of mine on this document. My sector chiefs drafted such documents as well. For the most part, Mr. Jure Radalj, who was the police sector chief, he was in charge of all uniformed police. He was the one to enter Vrlika first, together with the army, and it was probably he who wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you've no reason to question the accuracy of this information, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no reason to do that. I was familiar with this report. No written document could go through my police administration without me seeing it, and it could not leave the Police Administration without me seeing it. It was simply my style of management, because I had to manage one of the largest police administrations in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer into evidence Exhibit 65 ter 1D2991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1725.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the decision of admission, of course, I asked myself what we did the last four minutes. The witness was quite clear that he established the police station. Now this document seems to support that. Is this in dispute in any way? MS. DE LANDRI: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why -- I'm sorry. Why is it not just the Bar table saying, I would like to Bar table the document which supports the establishment of this police station, as stated by the witness? That takes approximately 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we have -- it's a matter which is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the issue going to the control of the territory, and that's -- that's the reason why I want to go into the particular document, itself. And if Your Honour bears with me, and -- I will get through this as quick as possible, and I will attempt to short-circuit the answers to the extent that they get off line. But that's the area that I'm getting into here, and I want to move this through as quickly as the Chamber does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cipci, with regard to the area that you -- when you set up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps I should admit this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, I don't see in the transcript at this moment the exhibit number. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that became Exhibit D1725.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cipci, when you established your police stations and your substations, at that time did the civilian authorities and the Police Administration take this area under control for the -- the occupied territory? And when I'm talking about the occupied territory, once you went in there and established these stations, did the Police Administration take those previously occupied areas under control -- under its control?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have in mind only my area of responsibility, that is correct. In order to normalise the situation in Vrlika as soon as possible, I had the chief of Vrlika, the civil representatives, with me. He accompanied me there, trying to establish civilian authorities, at the same time as I was setting up the police instances there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, let's move on. Later on that day, after establishing control in Vrlika, we read from your statement that you moved into Knin. And I'm addressing you to paragraphs 6 and 7. And you first moved to Kijevo, as you say in paragraph 7, then on to Knin. Now, did you do that, Mr. Cipci, because you understood that even though Knin was outside of your area of control, that Mr. Cetina's MUP personnel hadn't made it to Knin yet?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will reply to this. When we entered Vrlika, given that we had to wait there for a while because there was combat, upon our arrival in Vrlika, the commanders of the HV who were there told me that Kijevo had been liberated sometime previously. I telephoned Mr. Cetina and I told him Kijevo had been liberated. In accordance with the former agreement, Did you send your police force to Kijevo? Mr. Cetina responded by saying, Cipci, I am sorry, but Kijevo is not within my area of responsibility. I did not respond to that, but instead I phoned Minister Jarnjak immediately. I repeated my conversation with Cetina to him, and I asked him for his permission for me to enter Kijevo with my force, since I was interested in seeing the police take over control over the liberated territories as quickly as possible. The minister agreed, and I issued an order to my police sector chief and went on towards Knin immediately, presuming that Knin would be in the same situation as Kijevo. This was later confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you then went back on to Knin, as we see in paragraph 7, and you noticed there was no military police, nor civilian police, and did you then take steps to bring the military police -- excuse me, the civilian police, the MUP, into Knin to secure that area as well?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in Knin, in front of the command, the Serb command, I encountered a number of Croatian soldiers and officers. In conversation with those officers, I was asked by them to bring in any type of police, be it civilian or military police, as soon as possible. They saw me wear the uniform of chief of police. I agreed with that, but at that point in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. So when you went into Knin on the afternoon of the 5th of August, HV --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. In the morning of the 5th of August, HV officers asked you to bring police into the town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were lower-ranking officers. I knew, personally, the brigade commanders who had entered Knin, especially Mr. Krsticevic, but these were some lower-ranking officers whom I meant in front of the former Serb Army command. He told -- they told me, Mr. Cipci, if possible, please make sure that a police force arrives. That is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, sir, then you did, in fact, consult with Minister Jarnjak and bring a police force into Knin - didn't you? - as reflected --

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not establish a telephone connection or radio connection with Zagreb from Knin. That is why I had to go back to Vrlika. And it is only then that I consulted with the minister. I sought approval to enter Knin with my officers. He approved that, and I issued an order to my police sector chief, Jure Radalj, to have a hundred policemen who had been readied before, since I had extra numbers of them, given the size of my police administration, to have them sent to Knin immediately. They arrived there. There was no electricity. There was no water. That's why late in the afternoon I sent a fire truck full of water and a generator, as well as a radio station, to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me cut you short. MS. DE LANDRI: Excuse me. Mr. President, may the witness be allowed to finish his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I would not oppose the intervention by Mr. Kehoe here, because he asked about a consultation with Mr. Jarnjak, and we were now already at whether there was electricity, water, what kind of methods or what -- that there was a fire truck that provided that and a generator. So the witness is really moving away from what was asked. And under those circumstances, and you certainly have listened to this as well, please try to focus on what is asked. And if Mr. Kehoe wants to know what kind of trucks brought water in, then he'll ask you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, either prior to this conversation with Minister Jarnjak or thereafter, did anybody in the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Jarnjak or Minister Moric, or anyone else, or the HV, try to prevent you from bringing these police officers or sending these police officers into Knin to secure the area?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to bring them in. Therefore, I could not have been asked and prevented to do that at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me show you a quick document on this score. And it's 65 ter 1D2990. And it is a 5 August 1995 report concerning the establishment of Croatian authority in the area of Vrlika-Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, with regard to this document, I don't suspect there's any objection to the document. However, I do want to ask a question from -- several questions from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. If the document doesn't speak for itself, of course, we should ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could take a look at this document, sir, it establishes, the -- as I noted, Croatian authority in Vrlika-Knin, and it's dated 5 August 1995, and it's from the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration, which is your administration. And it notes the 10th Police Station. Before I get into this document, Mr. President, if there is no objection, I would just offer it into evidence and begin to discuss it as an admitted exhibit. MS. DE LANDRI: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1726.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1726 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, two questions with regard to this document, beginning in the first paragraph. And there's a report back from -- it says: "We are reporting in the afternoon hours of 5 August 1995, officers of the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration entered the settlements of Vrlika, Kijevo, Civljane, and Knin and established civilian authority in the same." Mr. Cipci, this comment "established civilian authority," what does that mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means, to me, what I already know, and that is that I brought the municipal head of Vrlika to Vrlika, itself. By virtue of his arrival, civil authority was established, and he was tasked with reconstructing it. As for the other locations, Vrlika, Kijevo, Civljane, some of these are small villages and hamlets around Vrlika, itself, and there were no civilian authorities there, per se, in the sense of any heads. In the former Yugoslavia, I believe these were local communes. As for Knin, civilian authority was established in a way that the Croatian government appointed its commissioner for Knin, who arrived there. As for whether he was there on the 5th or the 6th, I don't know that for sure, but I met him on the 6th in Knin. This was Mr. Petar Pasic. Regarding the part referring to police officers, it is not in dispute that we set up a substation in Vrlika, which is a substation of the 10th Police Station. That is why this letter to the HQ was sent by the commander, Marko Bilobrk, who was in charge of the 10th Police Station. He wrote this report on his behalf and sent it to the Povratak headquarters, which was headed by Josko Moric. It is also not in dispute that we entered with our employees into Knin and Kijevo. They --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me cut you short and move to the next question. When we're talking about establishing civilian authority, does that mean that the Croatian constitutional order was restored?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, when Vrlika is in question, this was the initial stage of establishing that order. A person who accompanied me to Vrlika on the 5th could not embody the entire concept of civilian authority, but he had been tasked that, in cooperation with the county prefect of Split and Dalmatia, to do everything that was necessary in the area of the town of Vrlika to establish civilian authority. In addition to the municipal head, other services needed to be established, since one person, of course, cannot embody the entire civilian authority structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, staying with this document and the last paragraph, it notes that: "Sanitation of the terrain is also underway and the same is being carried out by members of the Civilian Protection, principally in the area of the town of Knin." Now, I note in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can move to another document. That is D606. If we can put that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This will come up in a moment, Mr. Cipci. It is a document that bears your name from 9 August 1995, and it notes the report on terrain clearance in the area of Vrlika. And you note that: "As regards clearance in the Vrlika municipality until today, 8 August 1995, please be informed that the terrain clearance (60 conscripts) has accomplished the most important tasks, including: Burial of bodies ..." And then it has to do with other items, livestock and animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes that it is six human bodies as well as other animals were, in fact, buried. So from these documents, Mr. Cipci, it is true, is it not, that the sanitation of the area was the responsibility of the MUP and the civilian authorities, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: Before Operation Storm began, during the meetings we had held with the minister, all these obligations, collecting livestock, taking care of livestock, sanitation and hygiene measures, all those was agreed to fall under the competence of the police. In addition to the police force, I had under me the entire Civilian Protection with their staff and equipment. I also had a strong firefighting force which also participated. A few days following Storm, there occurred certain misunderstandings about livestock, because subsequently, Minister Susak authorised military units to collect livestock as well. This was a cause of disagreement between the police and members of the army, in terms of collecting the livestock, which may be irrelevant at this point. But, in any case, we did implement this. Since I was familiar, through my conversations with Mr. Petar Pasic, that he lacked either staff or equipment to do anything of that sort, therefore I sent in my Civil Protection men and firefighters to be of assistance regarding the tasks which were necessary to do in order to normalise life and the situation in this area, which was not under my competence. It was far simpler for me to do that in Vrlika. I cleared up things there in a mere two days, even the traffic signs along the road between Vrlika and Sinj. Hence, life in Vrlika became quite normal very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me shift gears with you, and I want to turn to paragraph 10 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: D1720 -- 1723, paragraph 10, if we can flip back to that, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 10 we are beginning to talk about reception centres, and you note that on the morning of the 5th of August, when you got to Knin, you set up reception centres, one for old people and children at the elementary school, and you also put one in for younger people near Sinj. Now, the allegation here in this case by the Prosecution, Mr. Cipci, is that these reception centres were merely a vehicle set up to remove the Serb population from the Krajina. What's your response to that, sir, given the fact that you were the ones that set these reception centres up in Knin on the morning of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not exactly like you are saying. I told them to open the reception centre in the elementary school hall. That morning, I saw a large number of people, women and children, on the street. They told me that they were Croats, which did not have to be the case. Maybe they were afraid, maybe they were Serbs and afraid to admit, but it doesn't really matter. I told them that all those who wanted to find shelter on that first day should be provided accommodation in the sports hall. At that moment, there was no water and electricity in Knin. We had the generator and we had enough water, and this was just to assist the population then, more than anything else. It was not gathering people for any other reason, because after a few days these people could leave of their own will. Let me give you an example. On the 6th or on the 7th, I got a telephone call from Celestin Srdelic, who is a good friend of mine. Later on, he became the ambassador of Croatia in Ljubljana, in its capital in Slovenia. And he asked me to help him locate his in-laws, because according to his information, they had remained in Knin. I told him, Cele, if they remained in Knin, then they're probably sheltered by my people in the police station or in the school. I went to the school or, rather, to the reception centre. I looked at the list. I found their names on it. I told them that -- Cele greeted them and that he would visit them within the next couple of days, and indeed he did. And when things normalised a little, they went of their own accord wherever they wanted to go. A large number of the Serbian population that remained in Knin found some shelter in the barracks of the international forces, which is at the entrance to Knin. And as far as I can remember, I suppose that this reception centre here accommodated a mixed population. I know that either on the 7th or on the 8th, the bishop of Sibenik came, Monseigneur Badurina, the late Monsignor Badurina came to visit. I was with him, and I believe that Mr. Pasic was with him at the time. In other words, those people were not accommodated in a camp. It was a reception centre set up in order to help those people within the next following days in a Knin which faced some rather difficult moments after it was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cipci, let me show you a document from 25 August that you authored concerning persons found in the newly-liberated area, sent to the attention of Mr. Franjo Djurica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 1D2992. If we can bring that up on the screen, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, take a look at this. It is a document that does not have your signature, but has your name at the bottom of it, authored by your office, with a stamp down on the lower left-hand side. Do you recognise this document, sir? And if you don't, do you have any reason to believe that it's not an authentic document emanating from your office?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there is any doubts about the authenticity of the document. After the liberation of the area, all those who had -- and many did, have relatives in either Split or Sinj expressed the desire to temporarily move in with them. Not far from Sinj, we established and opened a reception centre for the same reasons and with the same motive that made us open the centre in Knin. We were just waiting for everything to be normalised for -- the supply with water and electricity could be organised. It was just a temporary provision until things got back to normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time we will offer into evidence 65 ter 1D2992. MS. DE LANDRI: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1727.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1727 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
