utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, looking at this document, it notes that 70 of the 75 Croats were put on buses and taken to relatives in Split and Sinj, and 5, if you go to the last paragraph, 5 persons of Croatian nationality were settled in a reception centre for civilians where the 35 elderly people of Serb nationality, residing in Vrlika, Otisic, Koljani areas during the occupation were also settled. What was going on here, sir? Why were some of these Croats put on a bus and sent to the coast, some put in the reception centre, and all the Serbs located at the reception centre?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croats who had relatives are the ones who probably left to live with them. Some of the Croats did not have relatives in the territory of Split, and that's why they probably wanted to stay in the reception centre, to be provided with food, water, and everything else. I suppose that the Serbs from Vrlika did not have any relatives, and that's why they went there. I don't see any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, why not leave -- just leave them in their homes, Mr. Cipci?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably because the conditions for life there were not such to be conducive to peaceful living. They were all under a certain stress, and that's how I explain it. I see an initial here. I believe that this is Jure Radalj's initials. He was the chief of the police sector. It says here the Police Sector in the heading, and it says also for the attention of Mr. Franjo Djurica, who was also with the Police Sector of the Ministry. That's why I believe that Jure Radalj is the author of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cipci. If I may change subjects again, and pardon me if these aren't directly related, they're just topics that you brought up in your statement. And I would like to shift to paragraph 12 where you talk about your personnel being detailed to the Kotor-Knin Police Administration and put under the command of Mr. Romanic. And you note in paragraph 12 that they were in five separate police stations. And if I can just briefly go back to your testimony this morning in response to my learned friend Mr. Kay's questions concerning your supplying those individuals. And you note that -- on page 23, line 11 through 13, that these were young lads, and you were trying to show them that they should not be afraid. So these young lads, these young policemen, I mean, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who were sent to assist over there were people from my police administration, which means that they came from the police stations that were covered by my police administration. We're talking about 12 or 13 basic police units, the border police, the traffic police. Those were my police stations. And the chiefs of the police sectors from these units selected people to go first to Vrlika, to the police station there, and also people who went to assist; first, the batch of 100 and gradually numbers that the minister required me to send. My chief of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me cut you short. Would it be accurate to say that the police officers that you sent to these five stations in the Kotor-Knin area under Chief Romanic, those individual officers that you sent were not from those towns that they were sent to, they were from another location; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have been sent from Makarska, Vrgorac, Split. I don't know where they hailed from, where the chief found those people. In any case, those were people who resided and worked in the territory of the administration of Split and Dalmatia. I had 12 towns and the city of Split under my command. I had approximately 3500 policemen under me. And he selected those that were sent. I had an agreement with Chief Radalj that people who would be in command of the police stations, in the places they were sent to assist, should be Serbs for an easier communication with people who remained there, and that's why he -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be accurate to say, sir, that when you were bringing these officers supplies, there were officers that were sent to this area, young men that were sent to this area, that were unfamiliar with the area around these police stations; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they didn't know the areas. They hailed from different areas. They may have been from Makarska, Split, or Vrgorac, for example. All the logistical matters for the entire police in the territory of the Knin administration should have been provided by Mr. Romanic. However, since I had been in charge of the first batch of the police officers and all the others, and I ordered them to be in permanent contact with my chief of the police sector because I wanted to be updated on the developments, and they let us know that they don't have any quality provisions for life. And for that reason, every time I paid them a visit, I loaded my Range Rover with all sorts of things and goods that people needed for everyday living, starting with toiletries, food, drinks, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let me cut you off there and move to another topic. And I'd like to talk to you, in paragraph 25 of your statement, D1723, concerning the re-establishment of the Split-Knin train line that my friend Mr. Kay talked to you about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go back to D1723, paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, if you could take a look at paragraph 25, Mr. Cipci, you're talking about the problems that came from the re-establishment of the Split-Knin train line and what happened for civilians when they came back to the area on 15 August 1995. And you were informed -- it says in -- I'm not sure exactly what the line is in the B/C/S, but on line 30 in the English, that: "My police officers told me that the citizens went all over the town and were taking everything they could get." So you were informed by your police officers that the civilians were in town, looting; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your strategy was to put your police officers on the train and prevent them from taking the looted goods onto the train and to leave them back in Knin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, why didn't you have your officers arresting those people while they were doing the looting in the town?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although they were formally my police officers, I could not issue any orders to them. The patrols were set up by Mr. Romanic. Whether my police officers were members of those patrols, I don't know, but in any case, they knew very well what was happening in the territory of Knin. They informed my chief of the police sector, and then the police sector chief informed me. And then in agreement with my chief, I told them to do what they did, regardless of the fact that that was formally not something that I could order them to do because that order could have only come from Mr. Romanic. I assumed that Knin, although not a big town, Mr. Romanic did not have enough police officers to form patrols to prevent and arrest everybody. He had my hundred police officers initially and nobody else. That was all. Later on, Mr. Romanic got assistance from Rijeka, Pula, and some other places, depending on how the ministry decided to replenish the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, at this time on the 15th of August, did your people, who were in communication with your headquarters, give you any idea of how many civilians were in town, looting?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A whole composition left Split. Hundreds upon hundreds of people that could get on the train did so because the ride was free, and whoever had the inclination to do so, went up there. It would be wrong for me to speculate on the numbers, but I assume that a lot of people got on that train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the previous answer just leaves me with one additional question which I'd like to clarify with the witness. Witness, you said that they knew very well what was happening in the territory of Knin. They informed your chief of the police sector, and then the police sector chief informed you. And then you said: "... and then in agreement with my chief, I told them to do what they did, regardless of the fact that that was formally not something" you could order them to do, and then you explained why. What did you tell them to do, what they - as you said - then did?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to cut you short, but it's in paragraph 25. But the witness can answer the Chamber's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no, whether that is the answer or not, I'd like to know, as a matter of fact, from -- I've read that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just giving the Chamber a frame of reference as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may raise some other questions. But you said you told them what to do, and that's what they did. Could you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ordered them to form a line on both sides of the train, to stand there, and when people coming to the railway station saw them, they would not dare put the things on the train. And it is true, when they -- and when people left, the railway station was full of things, furniture and stuff. They left everything behind. And I suppose that, on the order of Mr. Romanic later on, all those things were removed from the train station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your policemen were there, and that's what we find in 25. As a matter of fact, your answer of what you told them to do, in 25, is that you told them, Let them do whatever they were doing. And then you didn't, therefore, as I understand, take any action to prevent or keep them off from looting before they arrived with their looted goods at the railway station. Is that how I have to understand this answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is as follows: Mr. Romanic must have known what was going on. I'm sure that he was informed, and he was duty-bound to possibly send patrols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question is: What did you tell them to do? Not what Mr. Romanic should have done, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told them -- my police officers told me what was going on in the entire area of Knin. They didn't ask me what to do, how to react. I told them to do exactly what they did. I could not give them an order to form patrols and to start patrolling the town. That was beyond my jurisdiction. I told them to do what they eventually did; to position themselves at the railway station and prevent from -- the looting civilians from taking the stuff away from Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was your authority to put them on the station at -- because you said you couldn't order them to do anything against the looting. In your statement, it says, I told them let them do whatever they were doing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could obey me, but, on the other hand, they didn't have to. However, given the authority that I enjoyed in the Police Administration of Split and Dalmatia, and given the fact that they had been my staff, they listened to me. But they did not listen to what I told them as an order, but as advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, why didn't you advise them to ask people they saw looting to stop looting? Why would you wait until everyone would be at the railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that at a certain moment I had to over-step my authorities and to embark on issuing orders that concerned the territory that I wasn't really responsible for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what I still do not understand is you say, Well, they would listen to me. Of course, I wouldn't give them orders because I had no authority to do so, but if I would advise them to do something, then they would do it. Now, apparently you advised them to go to the railway station, and you did not advise them to see what they could do about stopping the looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, given the number of them who were present at that moment, objectively, they could not have done much. The number of people who had arrived on the train was huge, and at that moment the only solution for me was to say what I did and for them to do what they did. If anything else was to be done, then that was within the jurisdiction of the chief of the Police Administration of Knin; nobody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you tell them to let them do what they were doing, the persons looting, don't stop them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say to them either/or. I just told them what to do next and how to do it, and they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that. One thing which is not entirely clear when you started explaining to us what happened with those goods, hundreds of people looting, leaving all the looted goods on the railway station, what happened to these goods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, I don't know. However, I assume that subsequently Chief Romanic ordered for the stuff to be collected and housed somewhere. I'm sure that those things did not remain sitting unattended at the railway station. As for the rest, the rest of the things that they had looted and tried to transport across my check-points where I was in charge, those people were criminally processed, and all the looted goods had been accommodated in Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking about -- you did not advise your police officers, who saw all these people leaving the looted goods on the platforms on the railway station or at the railway station, you didn't advise them to get them together and to -- and you just left it to see what Mr. Romanic would take for an action. Did you communicate with Mr. Romanic what would be a wise thing to do at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not talk to Mr. Romanic. I simply -- I considered him competent enough to be able to do in his area what was possible. It would have been out of order for me to suggest anything to a colleague. This may have been misunderstood, and that's why I didn't talk to Romanic. I suppose that he was wise and competent enough and that he would do whatever was necessary. Maybe he did; I don't know. Maybe you should ask Mr. Romanic whether he did something with the police forces at his disposal at the time. I sincerely doubt that he could do much or that he could establish enough quality patrols, with the number of men that he had at his disposal at the time, to prevent looting in the area. I'm sure -- or, rather, I assume that he did undertake some steps. I did -- I cannot believe that he let things go in that way, because if Romanic's police stopped maybe 50 people of all those who had arrived on the train, of the hundreds that had arrived on the train, the rest still escaped control. It would be unimaginable to expect that they could control every street, every house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, I wasn't asking you about what would have been reasonable or not for Mr. Romanic to do. My question was focusing on a different matter. You considered it within your possibilities to advise your police officers to go to the railway station, with the effect which is described in your statement, that everyone left his looted goods on -- in or around the railway station, but you thought it would be over-stepping your authority to give a phone call to Mr. Romanic saying, Well, a lot of looted goods are on the platforms. Could you please take care of that. You would consider that to be inappropriate to do in the circumstances. Is that correctly understood, and also that you, for that reason, didn't do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I simply said that it seemed inappropriate of me to warn Mr. Romanic that he was duty-bound to send out patrols to prevent looting. I didn't mean to say that it would be inappropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether you communicated with Mr. Romanic that looted goods were left on the railway station, and I understood part of your answer to be that it would be beyond your authority to inform Mr. Romanic on the presence of those goods, which might, well, create a problem because they were left behind, they belonged to other people. That's what I understood to be your answer, why you did not communicate the results of the activities of your men on the railway station to Mr. Romanic. Is that misunderstood or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You partially misunderstood me. It was not outside of my competence to warn him as to what had happened, but I was quite positive, as I am now, that the policemen under his authority, who were my policemen after what happened, that they informed Mr. Romanic of the whole situation. It seemed in excess for me to separately warn him of that, because there were a number of my policemen there. They definitely notified their commander, Romanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you advise them to inform Mr. Romanic? Did you say, One of you go to Mr. Romanic, tell him what we found here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know that because, for the most part, my sector chief, police sector chief, communicated with him. According to my order, they had to be in permanent contact with him. This police chief was Mr. Jure Radalj. I personally did not say anything to them because I did not have standing communication with them. I communicated with my sector chief, and he, in turn, communicated with his subordinates. There is a very strict hierarchy, in terms of subordination, in the police, and I had no need to contact directly with the various police officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you write a report on this action taken or advised by you to Mr. Radalj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that a report was drafted by my police sector chief. It's a minor activity in relation to the entire police administration. And the chief was not supposed to deal with such small issues. I would not be able to recall in this much detail unless there was a report drafted by the sector chief in the form of an Official Note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not inform your chief about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not draft any reports about that, and I suppose it was done by Jure Radalj, my sector chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, who was not informed, at least not by you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, I'd like to follow up on an a answer that you gave to the President, and that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Chamber and counsel at page 55, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- where you note, talking about these items: "I'm sure that those things did not remain sitting unattended at the ray way station. As for the rest, the rest of the things that they had looted and tried to transport, of course, crossed my check-points where I was in charge. Those people were criminally processed, and all the looted goods had been accommodated in Split." And with that in mind, sir, if I could turn to D989, which is a report by you dated 24 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up on the screen, D989.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Cipci, this is a report 24 August 1995 to Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page, paragraph 3, second page in English and second page -- excuse me. If we just look at the second page in Croatian, and then we can flip back so that Mr. Cipci can see how it is designated at the end, if we may, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Cipci, it's got your name with a stamp on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can, Mr. Registrar, if we can remain on the page for English and flip back to the first page in the Croatian and go to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you note: "Until 23 August 1995, 11 cases of unauthorised removal of movable property by others than the owners were reported, the perpetrators of which were in three cases HV members, who were handed over to be further dealt with by the military police, in six cases the goods were confiscated and a criminal report was submitted against the perpetrators (in one case the perpetrators were brought before an investigative judge). In the other two cases, a criminal investigation is underway." Now, you noted for us in the quoted transcript that I just referred back to you that the looted goods had been accommodated in Split. Now, was that your -- the normal practice, to take looted goods and bring it to a warehouse in Split?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen. All goods seized at my check-points were included in the regular procedure alongside those who had appropriated them. We had to take those goods somewhere, and that's why we agreed with the harbour-master in Split to be arranged that a warehouse be provided for us to store those goods, because I couldn't give this away as presents or sell it. It had to be preserved as evidence should there be a criminal proceedings, and only upon the conclusion of such cases, one could deal with such goods. That is to say, the police could not use the goods of its own accord. It was tasked with storing and preserving those goods as evidence until any relevant cases may be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Cipci, to your knowledge, what ultimately happened with those goods that were sent down to this warehouse in Split? Were they destroyed, were they given back, were they sold? I mean, what happened to this stuff?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the fate of the goods is something I don't know. When I left in 1997, those goods were still kept by the police. I believe all the proceedings moved forward very slowly following the initial criminal reports. It should be checked with the public prosecutor, the state attorney as he's called now, about the number of cases instituted against civilians, and with the military prosecutor about the cases against military personnel, and how many of those cases were concluded. All I know is those goods were still in storage in 1997 when I retired. As for what happened with them later, I don't know. It's probably gone to waste by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, let me stay with this document and use it as a transition point to yet another topic and concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could I seek first -- you said they were still in that warehouse. Was there a list made of what was stored in that warehouse? Was a register made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond? When the goods were seized at police check-points, the police made lists of seized goods, and these were official lists used as a basis for criminal reports to the prosecutors. The lists were attached, and a note was made. The goods were stored and assigned designations referring to the persons who committed those offences, and relevant numbers. In case any proceedings were to be instituted, this ensured that we could access those goods relatively quickly in relation to each and every perpetrator. Each item has its own number used to locate it and reference it to -- reference it to the person against whom a criminal report was submitted or proceedings instituted against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In that warehouse, a list -- a complete list was kept of what came in and what went out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That warehouse was under police supervision as well as the supervision of the northern port storage management. The goods could not leave the warehouse without police -- without a police approval, and they did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's nice to know, but it was not what I asked you. I asked you whether there was a list, and who would then give approval with or without such a list is another matter. Was there a complete list of everything stored in that warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a complete list of all the goods that were seized, and only on the request of a court, items would be shipped, if the court wanted to see it as evidence. I don't know, though, how many proceedings were instituted based on our criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, I asked whether there was a complete list. The answer, apparently, is, Yes, there was. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to move to another topic, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could just move to another document, but stay with this document, Mr. Cipci, and staying on paragraph 3. And you note in this paragraph that three perpetrators of which -- excuse me, the perpetrators of which were, in three cases, HV members which were handed over to be dealt with by the military police. So I take it from this report, Mr. Cipci, and your prior testimony, that the seizures -- these seizures were made at check-points and that the HV soldier, upon being detained, was handed over to the military police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So your people at the -- I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. At the very check-point, that is where they were handed over. We did not take them to Split. If there were no military policemen on the site, we would call some of them in, and at that check-point the perpetrators would be handed over to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Cipci, if I can understand your procedure well, your police officers, at the check-point, would stop and detain HV soldiers that they suspected of looting, and if there was no military policemen present, you would call for a military policeman to come to the check-point to take custody of the HV soldier that you suspected of looting. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I might have one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought I was going to go into this topic much further, but given the answer that I just received, I am not going to do it. Before the break, Mr. President, if -- I must say it has nothing to do with this witness, and he can certainly hear it. There was a procedural issue, and I take us back to when Mr. Margetts was still here. So harken back to Mr. Margetts. When we had some discrepancies concerning some documents and translations, I'm sure it's vivid in your mind, Mr. President; I completely forgot about it. In any event, we had these documents, we had Bar tabled them, Mr. Margetts had no disagreement, but we did re-up the transcripts. I will consult with the -- Mr. Waespi at the break concerning these documents, but the fact of the matter is that there were a series of documents in there that slipped through the cracks that have to do with this. But it has -- I'm not going to go into them with this witness, and I will talk to Mr. Waespi about it at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we will hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further. Then I would suggest that we first take the break, but I would like to deal with a matter briefly in private session, a matter totally unrelated to your testimony. Therefore, I would invite Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom, and I invite the Registrar to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break until 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I had one last document that related to the past questioning. It's a report by Mr. Cipci. I've talked to Ms. De Landri, and she's got no objection to the admission, and it's 65 ter 1D2993, a report of Mr. Cipci, 2 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to Bar table that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And just keeping in the sequence with this witness, I think it would be easier for this Chamber just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that will be Exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1728, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be marked for identification. If, Mr. Registrar, you could take care that we can get it on our computers, then we'll have a look at it, because no blind admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, next in line. Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Kuzmanovic, any questions for Mr. Cipci?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cipci, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Cipci. We'll be communicating in the same language, which will compound the interpreters' lives even further. That's why I'm going to ask you to be as low as possible in answering my questions, and also to try and make a little pause after my question, which will give the interpreters time to interpret my question. I will do the same, although I suffer from the same diseases as you, Mr. Cipci; namely, I speak very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the Registrar to put P497 on the screen for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, you're going to see a document that has already been admitted in evidence. This is Josko Moric's order about the establishment of the Povratak headquarters. In your testimony so far and in the documents that we've seen, there is a very common reference to the Povratak operation. Given your experience and the job that you had, could you please be so kind and tell us and the Trial Chamber about the Povratak operation. What was its purpose? What actions were taken within the framework of Povratak?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Povratak headquarters was established within the Ministry of the Interior, and it was headed by the assistant minister of the interior, Josko Moric. It had just one goal, and that was for the Croatian police, the civilian police, immediately upon the completion -- or, rather, upon the liberation of certain areas, comes to that area in order to ensure everything that police, under the Law on the Ministry of the Interior, is duty-bound to do. That's why police officers were supposed to participate in that operation. Those were uniformed police that were supposed to keep public law and order. They were supposed to ensure lawful integrity of individuals in the area. Also, the crime police sector also had to participate in that operation. When they learned about the perpetration of crimes, they were supposed to file criminal reports to the public prosecutor and process the criminals. There was also the Service for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. That was an intelligence service that was supposed to carry out an entire analysis of the developments during the occupation in order to bring to justice all those who participated in the armed rebellion and also in order to control, from the point of view of the Intelligence Service, what the situation was like after the liberation. There were also analysts who were supposed to record that all in computers so that the Ministry of the Interior could have complete documentation. There were also two services involved, the Civilian Protection and the Fire Brigade, that were part of the police administrations. They were supposed to provide logistics that fell within the purview of their services. And all that was necessary for the normalisation of life in the area. And then we also have the logistics for the police administrations. That was supposed to provide support to all the other services. And also there were supposed to be typists who were supposed to type minutes, records, reports, and so on and so forth, everything that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There's no doubt, Mr. Cipci, that it was a complex operation, a complex endeavour, a complex action, which obviously involved a large number of civil servants and public services. They were all necessary in order to achieve results?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The main burden should have been borne by the Government of the Republic of Croatia. It had to provide a maximum logistical support, funding, and personnel in order to implement the functioning of the civilian authorities. Due to the lack of people who would have been elected in elections, we sent commissioners who were discharging duties until the next elections. For example, in Sibenik we had Petar Pasic, who was the commissioner of the government. He was supposed to be in charge of the civilian authorities, and he had to make sure that the civilian authorities functioned. Without the help of the government, he would not have been able to do much, if anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The title of this broad operation was "Return" -- "Povratak." As a participant in the events, how did you understand the title of the Action Povratak or "Return"?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its very title suggestions that conditions had to be put in place for all those who had fled from the area on the eve of Storm, and there were lots of those who did. I'm talking about Serb citizens. Conditions had to be put in place for their return. Also, conditions had to be put in place for the return of the Croatian inhabitants of the area who had fled or had been expelled during the occupation which lasted for three or four years. You have to know that a large number of Croats were forced to leave the area, to move out from the area, because they were expelled. Their residential buildings and offices and workshops were destroyed. So conditions had to be put in place for the return of both groups. That's why the civilian authorities and the police powers had to function. That's why the headquarters were formed with the Ministry of the Interior. That was supposed to ensure all the conditions for the normal work of the civilian police. And then if that functioned as well as it had to, the police would provide for the normalisation of life in the area so that all the former residents of the area, those who had been either chased out or fled, or those who fled on the eve of Storm, could be returned. How things developed, we all know, thank God.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document, Mr. Moric's order that was sent to the Police Administration, is dated the 3rd of August. You can see that. We will all be able to see that if the Registrar scrolls the document down. The document is dated the 3rd of August, 1995, which means that it was sent before the beginning of Operation Storm. Mr. Cipci, I'm going to ask you this: How come that this document actually orders all police administrations, including yours, the Police Administration of Split and Dalmatia, where you were chief, why is it requested from all the police administrations to establish special headquarters which would be independent from the organisation of work within the Police Administration or with a view to provide for the Operation Povratak?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, as much as needed. This was done because the system of work in the police administrations during the war was such that we often had major actions that surpassed the regular policing duties that would have taken place under normal circumstances. In order to carry out such major actions, we always set up special headquarters, dedicated headquarters. That was one of the biggest, if not the biggest, action for all the police administrations, because it required a lot of people. And the idea was for the job to be done as well as possible. That's why the police administrations were ordered to establish their sub-headquarters that would have the same task, and that was all supervised by the main headquarters with the Ministry of the Interior, headed by Mr. Josko Moric. Therefore, the entire structure of the police was just as I'm telling you. It was identical, as you look at the hierarchy, and what existed at the top was reflected at the bottom. Identical headquarters were established at the lower levels, containing officials of the Police Administration, and, at the top, those were officials of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, Mr. Cipci. You were appointed in 1993 as the chief of the Police Administration of Split; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before that, for 33 years, if I'm not mistaken, if I did my math well, you were a judge at various levels in various courts. You were an investigating judge, a magistrate, an appeals judge; am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This means that you were trained to apply and protect law and the legal order of your state?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is part of my upbringing that I received at home, and then I was trained to abide by the laws, after so many years of working in courts. That's the only way you can live, that's the only way you can act and behave. And in factual terms, that was one of the reasons why I accepted Minister Jarnjak's offer to join the police from my court duty, because I assumed that in the turbulent times and in the war times, I could do most for the city of Split and the county of Split and Dalmatia if I assumed the duties as the chief of the Police Administration. And I believe that I did not make a mistake in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, while you were serving as a judge and later on as the chief of the Police Administration, did anybody put any pressure, did anybody try to influence you, did anybody suggest to you that you should turn a blind eye to certain illegal actions, unlawful doings, that you shouldn't process certain perpetrators of certain crimes, or not to apply policing methods that fell within your purview? Has anybody asked you to do that?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, this did happen, but just once. That was while I was still a very young judge, working in a very small court, and the prosecutor insisted on me passing on a judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. I'd be interested in pressure put upon the witness during his activity as a police officer or whether this ever happened in the past in his career. I thought your question was focusing on the -- not on the latter, but on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if it only happened when you were young, then there's no relevant incident that took place which we should hear about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, the gist of my question was about the duties that you discharged, the duties as the chief of the Police Administration, which involved events after Operation Storm. Were there any pressures there?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were never any pressures put on me, because at the very outset, at the very beginning, I informed the minister and all the assistant ministers to whom I wasn't subordinated - I was subordinated only to the minister - that it was out of the question for me to carry out of any of their orders if I deemed that that order was against the law. And the minister knew it only to -- well, I was by far the oldest civil servant within the Ministry of the Interior, I was well respected, and nobody ever dared suggest to me to do something that in my view would have been illegal or not strictly within the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the environment where you worked, where you had all your contacts, did you hear from somebody else that there was a plan according to which there should have been a planned action to expel the Serbian population from the newly-liberated area and to prevent their return to that territory?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard you about that in the media. That's the first time I became aware of that, but that -- I believe that that happened only when the proceedings were opened before this Tribunal. Before that, I never heard any such thing, nothing to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, Mr. Cipci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Ms. De Landri, are you ready to start your cross-examination? MS. DE LANDRI: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. De Landri. Ms. De Landri is counsel for the Prosecution. Cross-examination by Ms. De Landri:

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cipci. My name is Adria De Landri. I'm counsel for the Prosecution. I have a few questions to ask you relating to Defence counsel's questions. You practiced law for many years; is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what areas you practiced in?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a junior judge, I worked in the Municipal Court of Omis. Omis is a town some 30 kilometres away from Split, and that's where I was in contact with all the judicial duties. I was in charge of civil law, criminal law, litigation, property law, everything that fell within the purview of the Municipal Court, the Municipal Court in Omis. There was me and the president of the Court, but he was exclusively involved in the civil matters, and I had to do everything else. And then I joined the Municipal Court of Split after a year. Then I was assigned to the litigation part. And then in the Municipal Court, Split, I was involved in civilian matters. After a year and a half, I moved to the County Court, which used to be District Court. Then I served as a first-instance court judge. But very often at the same time I would be involved in criminal cases, especially during the summer months, when most of the judges would be on vacation. I never went on vacation during the summer. I split -- I live very close to the sea. I didn't have to go to have summer vacation. So the president of the Court and I would be in charge of cases involving grievous bodily harm, murders, killings, and that's when I was in charge of such cases. And then for a year and a half when there was a back-log in white-collar crime, for a year and a half I worked as an investigative judge, and finally I ended up as the president of an Appeals Chamber for matters of -- for civil matters. And that's where I worked for the next ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the process by which you became a judge? Let me clarify my question. Were you appointed or were you elected?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chiefs of police administrations were appointed by the minister. I must say, though, that the minister negotiated with me for about seven months, trying to persuade me to leave the court and start working as the police chief. As I said a moment ago, that it was my assessment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Listen to the question. Is the process by which you became a judge, "were you appointed or were you elected as a judge?" I take it -- MS. DE LANDRI: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. De Landri, I earlier denied an objection against Mr. Kehoe intervening. If the witness is not responding to your question, you can take him back to the issue you did put to him. Could you tell us whether you were elected or appointed as a judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a judge? I thought I was being asked as the chief of police. As for me being appointed a judge, I was elected by the Town Assembly and confirmed by the Croatian Parliament. Judges were not appointed in our country at the time. I was elected. I was elected by the Parliament of the then Republic of Croatia, which was part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, since the judiciary was within the republican purview. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And was that true for your entire judicial career, that you were elected?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the period. As of the moment when I was elected as the judge of the Municipal Court, I was elected by the Municipal Assembly, later on the County Assembly, and all the way to the Parliament. Later on, when I joined the County Court, I was directly elected by the Parliament following a proposal of the current justice minister of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I just want to briefly direct your attention again to your legal career. Based on the description that you gave the Trial Chamber, would it be fair to say that you never practiced law in the area of what could reasonably be termed "military law"?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the circumstances, I also acted as a judge of the Military District of Split for reserve commissioned and non-commissioned officers, because I had also completed a reserve officers school. I held a rather high reserve rank by virtue of which I was also appointed the judge of the Split Disciplinary Military Court in charge of reserve COs and NCOs in cases of breaches of discipline. That was my point of contact with military law, in addition to what I had been required to learn while I went through the reserve officers school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me try and take you back to your career as a practicing attorney. Did you ever practice in the area of military law before you became a judge?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never was a practicing attorney. I was only a judge, and I didn't deal with military law, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You testified earlier this morning, and I believe this is at page 7 of today's transcript, and it's lines 7 through 25, you said: "Obviously, I studied the laws that were relative to the system in the work of the Croatian Army. I was interested in finding about the relationship between the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence. And it was because I studied all that, I arrived at a conclusion very easily, because it is explicitly stated in the laws that a garrison commander has no authority whatsoever over the combat units deployed in his area." Can you cite a regulation or a statute that you base that statement on?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about a detail. I cannot answer that 15 years later. But I had the entire body of law at my disposal. We had all the existing regulation and laws of the former Yugoslavia in our judicial library, as well as in the Police Administration. I had an easy access to all laws and bylaws which had to do with the Croatian Army, the Croatian police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you start describing exactly what was in the library, the question simply was whether you can cite a regulation or a statute, and you told us that at the time you may have focused on it, but at this moment you're not able to do so. And that, I think, answers the question, Ms. De Landri. Or would you like to further know exactly how you got books from the library? Then please proceed. MS. DE LANDRI: But I would like to seek clarification on -- the witness did --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You did testify, Mr. Cipci, with some certainty, even though it was a few hours earlier this morning, about the authority that -- you gave a rather definite statement about the authority that you believe Mr. Cermak had over -- military authority that he had, and I'm just wondering -- now your statement -- the testimony that you've just given right now seems to be somewhat at variance with the very definitive statement you gave this morning. Can you describe why or explain why there is that variation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps explain what the variation is, as I'm unable to understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. De Landri, what the witness said earlier today is that after having studied the law, he arrived at the conclusion, and even very easily, because it is explicitly stated in the laws, that a garrison commander had no authority whatsoever, so that's the conclusion he arrived at when he had studied all that, whereas the witness now tells us that he can't cite, after 15 years, any specific. There is not a real variation in not remembering now what was at the basis of the conclusion at the time. I think what you'd like to establish, at least it seems to be the point you want to make, is that the witness at this moment cannot give a clear quote from the law on something he stated this morning, and that is now -- that is at least clear, that point is clear. If you want to further explore the matter, of course, please to so, but the evidence on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presiding Judge, if I may, I'd like to provide a very brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I leave that in the hands of Ms. De Landri, whether she'll invite you to do so, because, Ms. De Landri, the legal texts dealing with the authority, not only of garrison commanders but of all kind of other officials, of course, have been discussed before this Chamber in quite some length, and I think the Chamber earlier has expressed that the knowledge of this legal basis for whatever authority is not irrelevant, but we don't have to go through all of that in detail. Therefore, if there's any specific issue that you'd like to raise with this witness, please do so. If it's just that you'd like us to know that at this moment there's no clear recollection on the legal texts on which he may have formed his conclusions at the time, right or wrong, that's -- MS. DE LANDRI: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. There's plenty of other material to turn to, so we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you deem fit, Ms. De Landri. MS. DE LANDRI:

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cipci, I'm going to ask you some questions now about the written statement you've given. MS. DE LANDRI: So maybe we can have the witness refer to Exhibit D1723?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And if I could direct your attention to paragraph 4. You refer to a meeting that was held in paragraph 4. Do you see that? Take your time.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can you recall when that meeting was?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, and it would be presumptuous of me to claim that I know the exact date so many years later. But, in any case, it didn't happen much before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you make an approximation?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten or fifteen days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you recall where the meeting was?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, the meeting was held in the Ministry of the Interior in Zagreb, in Savska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. All chiefs were called to that meeting who had to do some work during and after Operation Storm; that is to say, the chiefs of those police administrations surrounding the occupied territory which was to be liberated: Split, Zadar, Sibenik, Karlovac, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber who else attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister, certainly, and I think his assistants were there. Mr. Moric, I believe, was there, as well as Mr. Smiljan Reljic. He was the assistant for the SZUP, and Moric was his assistant for the basic duty police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say "the minister," you're referring to Minister Jarnjak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Minister Ivan Jarnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So tell us, in as much detail as you can recall, what was discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting, we received instructions and orders of the minister specifying what we were duty-bound to do. Each police station and administration had to provide crews and officers for the police stations within their areas of responsibility and, in addition to that, provide a certain number of policemen which were supposed to assist the respective police stations in order to normalise the situation throughout the area. The minimum specified was 100 policemen, in addition to those who were supposed to staff the police stations in the area that was to be liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And, specifically, what instructions did you receive about what your role was to be at this time?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role or that of the police? My personal or of the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your individual, professional role in this capacity.

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My professional role, as the chief of a police administration, was to issue orders to my subordinates to do their part of the work and that they be ready for the beginning of Operation Storm. Save for myself, no one else knew the date and hour of the commencement of Operation Storm in my administration. I was the only one who was notified, and it is then that I issued the necessary orders. However, they had to undergo all the necessary preparations before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And who -- specifically, who did you receive your instructions from?

utterances.speaker: IVO CIPCI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who did I receive instructions from? As I said, I received instructions and orders from Minister Jarnjak, and then I, in turn, issued orders to the chief, Jure Radalj, who was chief of the sector of the police force, who had to provide staff for the substation in Vrlika and those who were supposed to assist them. MS. DE LANDRI: Mr. President, this might be a good time for a break in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I inquire as to how much time -- I know that you just started, but nevertheless just to have a -- and this is not in any way to -- an attempt to intimidate you, not at all, but could you give us an impression as to how much time you'd need?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could activate your microphone. MS. DE LANDRI: Oh, sorry. Between two and three sessions. Between two and three sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it's too early to ask the other parties. On from tomorrow - and, of course, the Judges may have some questions as well - we're not sitting for quite a period of time, so if you could think it over, whether there's a possibility to fit it into two or even a bit less, then in view of the substance, it might well be that we conclude the testimony of the witness tomorrow, which would be highly preferable. If there's no other matter, then we'll adjourn. And, Mr. Cipci, I'd like to instruct you again that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether given already, yesterday, or today, or still to be given. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom, because we adjourn, and we'll resume on Thursday, the 15th of October, at 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
